algorithms: Initialization by measurement and real-time feedback
key_findings: Demonstrated universal control of a six-qubit processor in silicon.
Achieved respectable fidelities for universal operation, state preparation, and measurement simultaneously.
Designed, fabricated, and operated a six-qubit processor with careful Hamiltonian engineering, a high level of abstraction for programming, and efficient background calibration.
State preparation combines initialization by measurement and real-time feedback with quantum-non-demolition measurements.
The six-qubit array is defined electrostatically in a 28Si quantum well of a 28Si/SiGe heterostructure.
Outer qubit pairs are measured using Pauli spin blockade (PSB).
Middle qubits are measured by quantum-non-demolition (QND) measurements with conditional rotations (CROT).
Initialization is based on measurements followed by real-time feedback, eliminating the need for slow thermalization or access to electron reservoirs.
Experimental runs of over one month were achieved with electrons remaining within the array continuously.
Initialization and measurement procedures yield visibilities of 93.5–98.0%.
All average single-qubit gate fidelities are between 99.77% and 99.96%.
Two-qubit gates are implemented by pulsing the barrier gate between adjacent dots, leading to ZZ interaction.
A controlled-Z (CZ) gate is implemented using CPhase evolution.
Automated calibrations correct up to 108 parameters.
Measured density matrices for two-qubit Bell states show state fidelity ranging from 88% to 96%.
Measured density matrices for three-qubit GHZ states show state fidelities ranging from 71% to 84%.
Heating effects leading to frequency shifts and reduced dephasing times are identified as a limiting factor for executing complicated quantum circuits.
The concepts used for control, initialization, and readout are estimated to be applicable to arrays twice as long and small two-dimensional arrays.
